title: Capability registry has an owner, has unregister, and has a real reset
wave: Spans two waves: commit 1 in wave 3 (unconditional), commits 2-3 in wave 4 (gated on M2-OQ2 from wave 1)
one_line: Rename the capability registry's `reset` to the truthful `invalidateAllCaches`, add a separate `resetRegistry()` that really does drop capability definitions, then give registered providers an owning `sourceId` and an `unregisterProvidersForSource()` so a suspended extension's contributions are actually released.
user_visible_effect: Commit 1 is invisible but stops a landmine: every future reader of the capability registry is told what `reset` actually does. Commits 2-3 are the visible part — after this ships, toggling an extension off in settings releases the capability providers it contributed instead of leaving them loaded, so a disabled extension stops contributing prompts, rules, hooks, slash commands, skills and tools. Today no toggle releases anything at all.
effort: S for commit 1, M for commits 2-3. Three commits, three PRs. Commit 1 is mechanical (8 import lines, 12 call sites, 1 comment) but the type checker will enumerate every caller for you. Commits 2-3 are ~40 lines of new registry code plus one line in a hot path.
risk: The single most likely way to get this wrong is the FORBIDDEN option: making `reset()` also clear the `capabilities` map. That looks like the fix and bricks the entire process silently — see the open_questions entry on why. The second most likely is a missed caller on the rename; the third is shipping commits 2-3 before wave 1 answers M2-OQ2, which leaves the attribution maps as permanently dead weight.
depends_on: WI-1 commit 1 (wave 2) — both add an owner-tagged teardown call to the SAME suspend branch of `reconcileExtensionSources`. Do not write that branch twice; whoever lands second EXTENDS it, never re-creates it. Verify at HEAD 808b365 that WI-1 has not already claimed it.
WI-0 (wave 1) — its M2-OQ2 answer ('is the capability registry extension-reachable?') decides whether attribution is worth building now. Commits 2-3 are gated on it; commit 1 is not.
blocks: WI-6 (wave 4) — the plan states WI-6 needs a settled tool-set story, and WI-5 is what settles ownership of the provider set.
WI-9 (wave 7) — unload needs a full resource inventory, and this item is what adds an owner to capability state.

plan_corrections.claim: (Plan does not state this) Implicitly, WI-5 assumes some live caller passes a `sourceId` to the capability `registerProvider`, so that `unregisterProvidersForSource` has something to unregister.
plan_corrections.verdict: FALSE — this is the most consequential thing the plan omits
plan_corrections.correction: There is NO per-source capability-provider registration anywhere in the repo. All 84 capability `registerProvider` calls are MODULE-LEVEL top-level statements in `src/discovery/*.ts` (agent-plugins, agents-md, agents, builtin-defaults, builtin, claude-plugins, claude, cline, codex, cursor, gemini, github, mcp-json, omp-plugins, opencode, skillshare, ssh, vscode, windsurf) — verified: no call site is nested inside a function. Extensions contribute to the capability registry by being READ at `load(ctx)` time, not by registering a provider. The `registerProvider` on the extension API (`extensibility/extensions/types.ts:1570`, `:1743`) is the MODEL registry's different function of the same name, which already takes a `sourceId`. Consequence: the `sdk.ts` suspend-branch call to `unregisterProvidersForSource` is INERT at ship time — it will be a Map lookup that always misses, because the map is always empty. It is forward-compatible scaffolding for WI-10, not a live fix. The two attribution tests must therefore drive the registry API DIRECTLY (register with a sourceId, then unregister), NOT through the TUI/suspend path, and the PR description must not claim toggling an extension now releases providers in practice.

A file that clears a module-level Map does not affect a sibling test file (verified: 2 pass / 0 fail, the second file still observed the pre-clear value). So `resetRegistry()` in `reset-contract.test.ts` cannot poison `provider-source-attribution.test.ts` or any other file. The plan's instruction that the two rows must be in that order is correct and the reason is now confirmed empirically: within a file, row 2's `resetRegistry()` would make row 1 fail if row 1 ran second.

open_questions: THE FORBIDDEN OPTION — do not do this, and know why. Making `reset()` also clear the `capabilities` map is the obvious 'fix' and it bricks the whole process. All 14 `defineCapability` calls are `export const x = defineCapability(...)` at module scope, and ESM evaluates each module exactly once — no later import re-runs them. So after the first `reset()`, `getCapability` and `loadCapability` return `undefined`/throw for ALL 14 capabilities across every one of the 12 call sites (`/clear`, resume-with-chdir, the reconcile loop, ssh session switches, marketplace install, …). It is a silent, stack-trace-free, process-wide failure. The ONLY sanctioned shape is: keep the fs-only function, rename it to say what it does, and add a separate `resetRegistry()` for the registry. The test row that catches this mistake is row 1 of `reset-contract.test.ts` — it passes on HEAD and fails the moment someone adds `capabilities.clear()` to `reset()`.

What should the fs-only function be renamed to? The plan says 'rename to be correct' but does not pick a name. Recommendation: `invalidateAllCaches()`. It is the honest sibling of the existing `invalidate(filePath, cwd?)` at `capability/index.ts:572`, it says 'caches' (plural) because it clears both the content and directory caches, and it does not collide with the existing `resetCapabilityForTests` at `:561`. The alternative `clearFsCaches()` collides in spirit with the already-imported `clearFsCache` alias from `./fs` at `capability/index.ts:11`. Either is defensible — but pick one and apply it to all 8 imports and 12 call sites.

Should the `resetCapabilities` local alias survive the rename? Recommendation: NO. All 8 files currently write `import { reset as resetCapabilities }`, and the alias is the second half of the lie — the name `resetCapabilities` is what makes the reconcile loop read as if it releases capabilities. After renaming, use the truthful name directly at all 12 call sites. This also forces you to touch `sdk.ts:3528`, whose comment ('resetCapabilities() clears the fs cache at those boundaries') must be updated to match.

Same `providerId` registered by two different sources — who wins? The plan does not address it and it is a real design hole. `providerMeta` (`:40`) is first-write-wins and `providerCapabilities` (`:37`) is keyed by providerId alone, so neither can distinguish two owners. Recommendation: mirror ModelRegistry exactly — `providerSourceByName` is one-to-one, last registration wins, and `registerProvider` evicts the previous owner from its set (copy `model-registry.ts:3010-3015`). Known accepted cost, identical to ModelRegistry's shipped behavior: if source A and source B both register provider 'claude' and B wins, suspending B deletes the provider even though A still declares it. Today this is vacuous (nothing registers per source), and it only becomes load-bearing when WI-10 makes the registry extension-reachable. If you would rather not accept that, the alternative is a refcount per (capabilityId, providerId) — but that is a second, invented shape, and the plan explicitly forbids inventing one.

Should `registerProvider` without a `sourceId` evict an existing source owner? Recommendation: NO — a source-less registration adds to the array but neither claims nor clears attribution. All 84 existing calls are source-less module-level registrations that run once at import; letting them evict would orphan a source-owned provider on any re-evaluation. This is a decision, not an accident; put it in the doc comment.

Gate question for the engineer: can the two new tests run BEFORE the Rust native addon is built? If yes, commit 2-3 can be validated this week instead of waiting on the build. Check it by running `bun test test/capability/reset-contract.test.ts` immediately after writing it. If it fails on the addon, say so in the PR rather than claiming test coverage you could not execute.

test_contract:
The suite defends one thing: the capability registry's exported lifecycle functions must do what their names say, and provider teardown must be scoped to exactly one owner.

Row 1 of reset-contract.test.ts defends a NEGATIVE contract and is the only thing standing between the plan and the one forbidden option. If it regresses, somebody has made the fs-cache invalidator also wipe the capability map — and the observable consequence is that `/clear`, resume-with-chdir, ssh session switches and the extension reconcile loop all silently stop resolving every one of the 14 capabilities for the rest of the process, with no stack trace, because ESM will not re-evaluate the module-level `defineCapability` calls. A consumer sees prompts, rules, hooks, slash commands, skills and tools quietly vanish and never come back.

Row 2 defends the forward contract: `resetRegistry()` must actually drop definitions. It is the row that fails on HEAD, because the function does not exist — it is the rejectable part of the fix, and it is what makes the name-and-behavior match enforceable rather than aspirational.

Row (a) of provider-source-attribution.test.ts defends the discovery contract: after a source is torn down, its providers must be absent from the RESOLVED list (`getCapabilityInfo(id).providers`) — the array settings UI and discovery actually read. A consumer sees a suspended extension's contributions disappear from the capability set instead of lingering. Asserting on the internal maps instead would pass while the resolved list stayed stale, which is the whole failure mode.

Row (b) defends the negative contract for teardown scope: two sources on one capability, one torn down, the other's provider survives. If this regresses, `unregisterProvidersForSource` over-deletes and disabling one extension silently strips another extension's contributions. This is the row that proves attribution is real rather than a single-owner special case.

Row (c) defends the cross-commit contract: the two commits do not regress each other. `resetRegistry()` must not disturb attribution, so a test suite that calls it still sees source-owned providers afterwards. If this regresses, commit 1 quietly breaks commit 2's cleanup path.

What a consumer sees if any of this fails is a capability registry that either leaks every suspended extension's providers forever (the status quo at HEAD) or, in the forbidden variant, drops every capability in the process. Both are silent; neither throws.
